summary:
UtopianEye is an interactive geospatial web application that unifies more than two decades of satellite fire records by harmonizing active fire hotspot observations across NASA’s MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP/NOAA-20) sensors.

As MODIS nears retirement, differences in spatial resolution (1 km vs. 375 m) and sensor sensitivity introduce artificial jumps into historical trends. UtopianEye resolves this challenge by aggregating detections into standardized 1 km fire-cell-days and applying a Bayesian-calibrated seasonal and regional harmonization model trained across 14 years of overlapping data (2012–2026). The platform equips users with an interactive satellite map, custom Area of Interest (AOI) drawing tools, a 26-year Year×Month Burning Activity Calendar, multi-year median anomaly detection, live FIRMS hotspot feeds, and CSV export capabilities.

This tool is vital because it establishes a continuous, sensor-agnostic fire baseline from 2000 to the present. By ensuring that historical comparisons reflect genuine ecological shifts rather than sensor transitions, UtopianEye empowers emergency managers, scientists, and land stewards to detect abnormal fire behavior, strengthen early warning systems, and improve disaster response worldwide.
details:
Project Details

What does it do or how does it work?

UtopianEye creates a continuous, 26-year active fire hotspot record (2000–2026) by harmonizing NASA’s legacy MODIS (Terra/Aqua) data with next-generation VIIRS (S-NPP and NOAA-20) data.

Because VIIRS has a 375 m pixel footprint compared to MODIS’s 1 km pixel footprint, raw VIIRS detections report 4–5× more fire pixels for the exact same fire events. UtopianEye harmonizes these records in two stages:

  1. Physical Gridding & Deduplication: Point detections are snapped to a standardized 1 km sinusoidal grid, counting unique fire-cell-days (whether a 1 km cell experienced burning on a given date). This eliminates spatial oversampling and overpass overlap.
  2. Bayesian Calibration: Using 14 years of overlapping standard-processing data (2012–2026), a hierarchical regional ratio model (block_month_ratio with empirical Bayesian shrinkage) learns month- and region-specific conversion coefficients (kkk) that map VIIRS counts to MODIS-equivalent values.
  3. Interactive Web Application: The harmonized dataset (over 1.4 million tile-month rows) is indexed in an in-memory DuckDB columnar engine and served via a FastAPI backend. Users can draw custom Areas of Interest (AOI) on an interactive satellite map, visualize seasonal patterns across a Year × Month Burning Activity Calendar, assess anomalies against a 10-year baseline median (2002–2011), view live near-real-time (NRT) hotspots, and export filtered data to CSV.

What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates Sensor Transition Bias: Solves the artificial jump in fire activity that occurs when transitioning from MODIS to VIIRS, preventing false disaster alarms.
  • Immediate Situational Awareness: Emergency managers can rapidly assess whether current monthly burning is normal, elevated, or extreme relative to a 25+ year multi-sensor baseline.
  • Flexible Area Selection: Allows instant querying across any custom bounding box or administrative boundary without needing GIS software.
  • Fast, Lightweight Processing: Columnar parquet storage and embedded OLAP querying deliver sub-second responses over millions of satellite observation records.

What is the intended impact of the project?

UtopianEye is built for emergency responders, forest officials, agricultural monitoring teams, and climate scientists. As MODIS approaches complete decommissioning in 2027, long-term environmental and fire tracking risks critical discontinuity. UtopianEye safeguards the historical baseline, giving decision-makers reliable early warnings and verifiable historical context to guide firefighting resources and policy.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.10, Modern JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3
  • Data Engineering & Backend: DuckDB (in-memory analytical query engine), Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX
  • Frontend & Visualization: Mapbox GL JS, Chart.js 4, KaTeX / responsive SVG components
  • APIs & Cloud Hosting: NASA FIRMS REST API, Mapbox Satellite API, GitHub, Render (cloud container deployment)

How is your project creative?

  • Physical-plus-Statistical Hybrid Calibration: Rather than applying a single naive conversion multiplier or a black-box machine learning model, we combined physical grid-cell daily deduplication with regional Bayesian shrinkage that gracefully handles sparse fire regions.
  • Static Flare Filtering: We developed an automatic spatial mask that uses historical fire type classifications to eliminate permanent industrial flares and gas vents from near-real-time data streams, preventing recurring non-vegetation fires from corrupting seasonal anomaly scores.
  • Dual-Data Architecture: Blends massive precomputed historical data (2000–2026) with live on-demand FIRMS API pulls in one responsive interface.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Orbital Drift & Overpass Schedules: Addressed the differences between Terra’s morning crossing and the afternoon orbits of Aqua, S-NPP, and NOAA-20, fitting models that preserve science-quality continuity.
  • Fire Type Diversity: Accounted for regional differences across fire regimes (e.g., small, dense agricultural stubble burns in northern agricultural belts vs. expansive forest fronts).
  • Accessibility & Color Vision: Selected perceptual, accessible color ramps (YlOrRd / Viridis gradients) for the burning calendar to ensure readability across all user groups.
